<pasted_content id="dc5b">
We're finishing my Anthropic take-home (Co-learn + Learn mode). Deadline: Oct 21, 9:00 AM PT. The prototype is deployed and feature-complete; main auto-deploys.

The repo moved out of iCloud Drive to ~/code/claude-co-learn (2026-10-19). Earlier transcripts live under other ~/.claude/projects folders; scripts/collect_transcripts.py already gathers from all of them.

Read first: docs/HANDOFF.md §0 (current status and next-session order), then docs/plan.md (Phase 4 and "Remaining for Dinakar"). The testing guide is docs/testing-guide.md. Skim docs/decision-log.md and docs/design-principles.md only as needed. CLAUDE.md is loaded.

Done last session: Learn-mode stories built from the topic; Learn lessons prefer strong sources; citation markers renumbered to match the sources shown; each lesson shown as soon as it's written (path 7s, lesson 14s, question 24s); testing guide written; transcript script fixed; repo moved.

This session, in order:
1. Manual testing support. I'm testing with docs/testing-guide.md (tiers 1-3). For each issue I report: reproduce it (live-check tools in web/scripts/e2e/, always in test mode), fix it with tests, keep typecheck/test/lint/build green, and commit and push in small steps. Ask me before any product or design change; small bug fixes are fine.
2. When I say so: run /rationale-coach for docs/design-rationale.md, then write the ≤8-minute video script and shot list, and pre-stage demo sessions in test-mode tabs.
3. Pre-submission: make the repo public (re-scan transcripts for secrets after collecting them), run python3 scripts/collect_transcripts.py, remove transcripts/raw/ from .gitignore, commit, do a final health check, and draft the Greenhouse text.

Working agreements: I own design decisions (give me options with a recommendation; log my decisions and reasoning in docs/decision-log.md, and ask for my reasoning if I haven't given it). Never print or commit secrets (web/.env.local); the site password is light security and fine to show. Keep live API spend modest (a few dollars). Give me the command for any bulk production delete. Keep docs/plan.md, HANDOFF §0 and docs/testing-guide.md current. Be economical with tokens: delegate broad searches, don't re-read large files you don't need, and keep updates short.

Start with a two-line status check, then wait for my first test report.
</pasted_content id="dc5b">

# CLAUDE.md — project context for Claude Code

## What this is
Dinakar's take-home for the **Full Stack Engineer, Education Labs** role at Anthropic.
Build a deployed prototype (using the Claude API) that enhances human learning and agency,
plus a written design rationale and a ≤8-minute video. Full brief: `docs/assignment-brief.md`.

Official deadline: **Oct 21, 2026, 9:00 AM PT**. Personal target: Oct 20. Expected effort: < 1 day; depth over breadth.

## Working agreements (important)
- **Dinakar owns the design decisions.** The evaluators assess *his* judgment in guiding Claude,
  not Claude's raw output. When a design choice comes up, present options with trade-offs and a
  recommendation — don't silently decide. Ask for his reasoning when it isn't stated.
- **Log decisions.** When Dinakar makes a meaningful design/technical decision, append it to
  `docs/decision-log.md` (date, decision, alternatives considered, his rationale).
- **Never commit secrets.** API keys live in `.env` (gitignored). Use `.env.example` for placeholders.
- Only commit/push when asked.
- Prefer simple and thoughtful over complex. Pick one specific user journey and go deep.

## Direction (2026-10-17)
Option B: **Co-learn**, a Claude mode where users do real work with Claude and get short, game-like learning moments
triggered by their work. Demo: a working professional training an ML model. See `docs/product-vision.md`.

## Key docs
- **`docs/HANDOFF.md` — read first in a new session: current status + next steps**
- `docs/design-plan.md` — **build blueprint** (architecture, tools, engine, data model, build order)
- `docs/design-principles.md` — Dinakar's design principles (don't change without proposing first)
- `docs/product-vision.md` — Co-learn experience, learning moments, pacing engine
- `docs/context-persistence.md` — storage and model-context plan
- `reference/research/` — research reports; `reference/ascii-characters.md` — character art
- `alternative-projects/` — archived ideas, not part of the submission

## Build conventions
- App lives in `web/` (Next.js 16; read `web/AGENTS.md` and `web/README.md` first).
- Shared contracts in `web/lib/contracts/` are frozen during parallel tracks; propose changes instead of silently editing.
- Before committing: `npm run typecheck && npm test && npm run lint` in `web/`.

## Repo layout
See `README.md`.
- [Site password is light security](site-password-light-security.md): don't flag or rotate SITE_PASSWORD; real secrets still never printed

Each block's opening and closing tags carry the same random id; the user never sees the id, so don't mention it when referring to the pasted text.

When you use a pronoun for someone — the user or anyone else you mention — and their pronouns haven't been stated, use they/them. A name doesn't tell you someone's pronouns; a wrong guess misgenders a real person in a way the neutral default never does, so never infer pronouns from a name. description: <one-line summary, used to decide relevance during recall>

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.

tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

schema.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

Reach for this when the task matches an available agent type, when you have independent work to run in parallel, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate it and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps. For a single-fact lookup where you already know the file, symbol, or value, search directly. Once you've delegated a search, don't also run it yourself — wait for the result.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }

  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

# Rationale coach

You are helping Dinakar write the **written design rationale** for his Anthropic take-home (`docs/design-rationale.md`).
The reviewers assess *his* judgment and perspective. A mostly-Claude write-up without his own reasoning fails the brief.
Your job is to **interview, organize, and edit**, not to author his opinions.

## Ground rules
- **His voice, his reasons.**
  - Every claim of *why* must come from something he says in this session, or from a decision-log row marked as his decision or approved by him.
  - Never invent motivations, feelings, or anecdotes.
  - If a section needs a reason he hasn't given, ask for it.

message.content: I chose Option B over A becuase I don't have the expertise in claude code myself to understand best how to design something like option A. Separately, I found the broader ambitions of Option B more exciting and compelling for me personally, as it is something I would actually use (in contrast with Option B). I chose a professional training a model as the demo journey because that is a use case I as a professional have and would benefit from learning from, so it would make it easier for me to understand the customer journey by actually being a customer of the product myself. Finally, in terms of the scope of this project, I initially designed it as a topic tutor, which is what I would get the most use out of. But the prompt was a little ambiguous with regards to whether or not the tool needed to teach people AS they were doing work with claude, so i decided to bifurcate it into two separate modes, for the different use cases - co-learn and learn. content.text:
Here's the draft. I read "in contrast with Option B" as a slip for Option A; tell me if I've got that wrong.

---

**1. Option chosen and why**

I chose Option B for two reasons. First, I'm not a Claude Code expert, so I wouldn't have the depth to design something like Option A well. Second, Option B's broader ambition excited me more, because it's something I would actually use myself.

That second point shaped the demo too. I picked a working professional training a churn model because it's a real use case for me. Training models is part of my job, and learning the concepts behind them would help me. Being a customer of my own product made the customer journey much easier to understand.

My first design was a topic tutor: pick a subject and Claude teaches it. That's the version I'd use most. But the prompt left open whether the tool had to teach people *while* they work with Claude. Rather than guess, I split the product into two modes:
- **Co-learn:** you do real work with Claude, and short, game-like learning moments come out of that work.
- **Learn:** you name a topic and Claude plans a short path of cited lessons and questions.

These are very different flow states with different needs. Someone in the middle of a task wants learning that stays out of the way, while someone studying wants structure. So users choose the mode that fits.

---

What would you change (tone, emphasis, anything missing or overstated)? Or say "good" and I'll save it and move on to section 2.

message.content: it sounds good

- What did you decide *before* building, and why principles first?
- How did you work with Claude: what did you delegate, what did you decide yourself, and how did you check its output?

  - **Reset:** start over easily as a new user.
  - **Test-traffic tagging:** your own testing stays out of the numbers.

content.text:
Here's the draft:

---

**2. Design and prototyping process**

I wrote my design principles before anything else. I think principles are the atomic unit you can expand into a solution: they capture why I want to solve the problem and how I want to think about it. Nine principles came first, then the product vision, then a design plan, and only then code.

I made the design decisions. Claude wrote most of the code and, at every choice point, laid out options with trade-offs. I picked one, and each pick went into a decision log with the alternatives (60+ entries).

How I checked Claude's work comes from a broader belief. As AI advances, it will get harder for people to follow every intermediate step it takes; that's why fields like interpretability exist. In that world, the most important thing to check is the final result. So I judged the prototype mainly by using the live website. I tested it in a real browser and played through it myself, and those sessions drove the second build round.

The playtest moment that changed the design most was when I got a question I couldn't answer, and the product had no way to help me learn it. Asking questions isn't enough; people need a path toward the answer. So I added:
- hints, "Teach me", and "Ask Claude" on every question
- slightly less credit after using help, with no penalty beyond that
- the answer revealed only after you've tried

That lets people at any level engage with the question-and-answer format instead of only those who already know.

---

Anything to change? One thing to check: the second paragraph ("I made the design decisions. Claude wrote most of the code…") is taken from how the decision log works rather than from your words just now. Keep it, or tell me how you'd put it.

Here's the rewrite. I kept your point about checking the final result and the playtest moment, shortened, since those answer the brief's questions. Cut them if you'd prefer.

---

**2. Design and prototyping process**

I started from my own understanding of how people learn. It comes from my background as a professional tutor and a long-standing personal interest in education and what actually helps people learn. I wrote that down as nine design principles. Then I had Claude check each one against peer-reviewed research, so the foundation rested on evidence and not only my experience.

Next, I designed the product experience myself and shared it with Claude. We went back and forth on whether it made sense, and I made the final calls. Every meaningful choice went into a decision log with the alternatives I considered (60+ entries).

Then I wrote a high-level engineering plan, drawing on my experience as a Staff engineer planning software projects: the architecture, shared contracts, and a build order that let parts of the work run in parallel. Claude carried out that plan and wrote most of the code.

Finally, I tested the experience myself in a real browser and played through it as a user. As AI takes on more of the intermediate work, I think the most important thing for a person to check is the final result, so that's where I spent my review time. Those playthroughs drove a second build round. The biggest change came when I got a question I couldn't answer and the product had no way to help me learn it. So I added hints, "Teach me", and "Ask Claude" to every question; slightly less credit after help; and the answer revealed only after you've tried. Now people at any level can take part, not just those who already know.

---

Good, or changes?

**3. How it enhances, not replaces, human agency**

Two of my core principles are "active application is the core" and "the user stays the decision-maker." Both mean the learner should be thinking about the problem, not receiving a firehose of information. At the real forks in the work, like which metric to optimize or where to set a threshold, Claude asks instead of deciding. Then it builds on the answer: "You picked recall, so I scored the models on that." If a choice is weak but safe, Claude goes with it and lets the real results show the consequence.

Making decisions uses a different part of the brain than taking in facts. It leaves people feeling empowered, not like a store of knowledge, and storing knowledge is something AI is increasingly good at anyway. I want people to come away better at judgment, the part that stays theirs.

Some of this is enforced by design, not left to the prompt. A learning moment is a tool call that ends Claude's turn, so Claude can't answer its own question.

The control I care about most is that help only comes when you ask for it. Hints, "Teach me", and "Ask Claude" are always there, but nothing appears unless the learner reaches for it, and the answer is revealed only after an attempt. That puts the learner in full control of the difficulty, including the choice to struggle through a problem on their own. Everything else is opt-out too: skip a question, save it with "Quiz me later", pick a guardrail level, turn down a boss, or simply keep typing and the question steps aside.

---

Good, or changes?

Here's the draft. One fact to note: the story now appears only in Learn mode, so I've worded it that way.

---

**4. Learning principles behind the decisions**

Three principles matter most to me, and each shows up directly in the product.

**1. Practice.** People learn by applying knowledge, not by reading about it. This principle covers several research findings at once, and it's why questions are the backbone of both modes. Learners recall the answer themselves before seeing options; multiple choice is only a fallback. Every answer, right or wrong, gets an immediate "why", because mistakes only help when they're explained right away (Kornell, Hays & Bjork, 2009). Bosses mix concepts from across the session, and concepts you struggled with come back in a later session.

**2. Adaptive difficulty.** Difficulty has a huge effect on engagement. People want material that feels hard enough to be worth overcoming, but not so hard that they give up, and the job is finding that balance for each person. The engine targets success rates by question type: 85–90% the first time you meet a concept, 75–85% in practice, 65–80% in a boss. It steps down quickly after a miss and ramps up slowly after successes. When a question is still too hard, help steps in: a hint, then a short lesson, then the question again.

**3. Reward.** Hard work should feel rewarded. XP, sounds, confetti, and level-ups that unlock themes celebrate success in proportion to the effort. Wrong answers get a soft sound and encouragement, never a penalty. In Learn mode, a serialized story adds a reason to keep going. Together they keep a positive feedback loop running: effort leads to reward, which leads to more effort.

---

Good, or changes?

Here's the draft:

---

**5. Measuring success**

For the product, success means it actually helps people learn. By the end of a session, people should be able to answer questions and apply the knowledge the product tests them on. That shows up in two ways: a high share of accurate answers, and how confident people say they feel about what they learned, measured with a short survey. The wrap-up already asks a quick "Did you learn something?"

For users, success also includes how they feel: whether they enjoyed it and want to keep using it. At scale, that's daily active users and return rates.

The first thing I'd check is adoption: whether people actually want to use it, and whether those who try it once come back. A learning tool nobody returns to can't teach anyone much. Next, I'd look at signals inside the session, which the `/insights` dashboard already tracks:
- **Accuracy against the difficulty bands:** consistently above target means questions are too easy; below means too hard. Early testing showed questions landing above the band, so they need to get harder.
- **Boss engagement:** how often people take a boss on versus decline or skip it.
- **Help usage:** how often people reach for hints, "Teach me", or "Ask Claude", and how they score with help versus without.

Together these show where to tune the experience to be easier or harder. The dashboard also measures delayed retention, comparing scores on a concept in a later session with the first, which is the clearest test of whether learning lasted.

---

Good, or changes?

The term is **Upstash Redis**, a serverless Redis database the app uses through Vercel's marketplace. Here's the draft:

---

**6. Scaling to millions of users**

The hardest part of scaling isn't infrastructure; it's that every learner is different. People need Claude to sound and speak to them differently, and they differ in how hard the content should be and how fast it should ramp up. One model serving everyone the same way won't work. The prototype already adapts difficulty per person with a small engine, but at scale I'd push further. First, I'd prompt the model to adapt as much as possible to each user. Then I'd add persistent personalization that carries across sessions, potentially using lightweight fine-tuning such as LoRA if prompting isn't enough.

The architecture is a reasonable starting point. The server routes are stateless, so they scale out easily; each user's state is a small JSON record in Upstash Redis. Costs stay low through prompt caching, a cheaper model (Haiku) for grading and hints, a pacing engine that is plain code with no model calls, and automatic summarizing of long sessions. A 10-minute session costs about $0.20–0.30 today. Rate limits and daily spend caps protect against abuse.

For a real launch, I'd change four things:
- **Infrastructure:** move off the free tiers of Vercel and Upstash Redis to paid plans, and load-test with many people using it at once.
- **Where it lives:** either build it directly into Claude's own products or ship it as a standalone product, not a separate demo site.
- **UX polish:** refine the design so each element sits in the ideal spot.
- **Model quality:** iterate on every stage of the experience so the questions, hints, and explanations are as good as they can be.

---

Good, or changes?

---

**7. Getting a sister team to adopt it long-term**

I read this question two ways: a sister team *using* Co-learn in their own work, or a sister team *building it into* their own product. I'll answer both.

**Using it.** I'd start by learning what the team works on and asking them to share a recent problem that was complex or ambiguous. Then I'd build a demo showing how Co-learn would have helped them work through that problem and learn along the way. A demo on their own real problem is far more convincing than a generic pitch.

**Building it in.** I'd go first to a team that builds custom Claude interfaces, since that's closest to our own work. My pitch: turning Claude into something game-like is likely to pay off well beyond learning, and every surface that adopts some of it multiplies the benefit. What I'd share:
- **The question cards** shown to the user, as code they can customize for their surface.
- **The game layer:** progress tracking, XP, and rewards, run by a pacing engine with a clear, tested interface. Adopting it means adding one tool and rendering the card.
- **The metrics:** the same telemetry and `/insights` dashboard, so they can measure learning from day one.

**Keeping it working.** I'd offer for our team to keep maintaining the shared infrastructure, while both teams share ownership of the user metrics and of whether learners succeed. Shared goals are what keep an adoption alive after the launch excitement fades.

---

lines: # Co-learn: design rationale
-> **Status:** sample draft scaffold.

-> **How to fill it in:** each section lists what the brief asks, the questions to answer, and raw material (facts and sources), followed by an empty **Draft** for your own words. Run the guided session with `/rationale-coach` in Claude Code. It walks you through one section at a time, asks for your reasoning, and drafts in your voice for you to edit.
-> **Target length:** about 2–3 pages in total (≈150–300 words per section). The video carries the demo, so this doc carries the *why*.
-> Prototype: https://anthropic-take-home-10-17-26.vercel.app · Repo: this one · Decisions in full: `docs/decision-log.md`
+Dinakar Guthy · Full Stack Engineer, Education Labs take-home.
+Prototype: https://anthropic-take-home-10-17-26.vercel.app · Decisions in full: `docs/decision-log.md` · Video walkthrough: _(link)_
## 1. Option chosen and why
-**The brief asks:** which option, and why.
-**Questions to answer:**
-- Why Option B over Option A, in your own words?
-- What made you re-scope from a "topic-to-game tutor" to Co-learn?
-- Who is the user, and why that journey (a working professional training a churn model in ~10 minutes)?
-**Raw material:**
-- Option B: broader and more open-ended (learning anything while working with Claude, not just Claude itself).
-- It plays to your strengths: you're not a Claude power user, so you couldn't build as detailed an Option A; B lets you apply learning-design ideas to real work.

-- You started from a topic-to-game tutor idea, then realized B is about learning *through AI-assisted work*, and re-scoped to Co-learn (the original is archived in `alternative-projects/learning-quest/`).
-- Target user: a working professional. Demo journey: training a churn model. Default session: 10 minutes, so reviewers can finish a full session.
-- Sources: `docs/decision-log.md` (2026-10-17 rows "Choose Option B", "Re-scope to Co-learn", "Target user").
-**Draft:**

I chose Option B for two reasons. First, I'm not a Claude Code expert, so I wouldn't have the depth to design something like Option A well. Second, Option B's broader ambition excited me more, because it's something I would actually use myself.

That second point shaped the demo too. I picked a working professional training a churn model because it's a real use case for me. Training models is part of my job, and learning the concepts behind them would help me. Being a customer of my own product made the customer journey much easier to understand.

These are very different flow states with different needs. Someone in the middle of a task wants learning that stays out of the way, while someone studying wants structure. So users choose the mode that fits.
## 2. Design and prototyping process
-**The brief asks:** your design and prototyping process.
-**Questions to answer:**
-- What did you decide *before* building, and why principles first?
-- How did you work with Claude: what did you delegate, what did you decide yourself, and how did you check its output?
-- What changed after you played with it yourself (your playthrough feedback)?
-- One or two moments where live testing changed the design.
-**Raw material:**
-- **Order of work:**
-  1. Research.
-  2. Nine design principles (`docs/design-principles.md`).
-  3. Product vision.
-  4. Design plan.
-  5. Contracts-first parallel build (5 worktree tracks).
-  6. Integration.
-  7. Live testing in a real browser.
-  8. Your playthrough.
-  9. A second build round.
-- **Decision log:** every meaningful decision with the alternatives considered (`docs/decision-log.md`, 60+ rows). Claude proposed options; you chose.
-- **Live testing changed the design:**
-  - Claude explained the "leak" before asking about it, so we added a "don't spoil moments" rule.
-  - No boss appeared within 10 minutes, so we added the milestone nudge.
-  - The miss feedback gave the answer away before the options, so it's now a hint first.

-- **Your playthrough:** "if I don't know the answer… there aren't mechanisms for me to learn." That led to the help tools (hints, Teach me, Ask Claude), less credit after help, and reveal only after an attempt.
-- **Your other playthrough changes:**
-  - **Boss exits:** the opt-in offer and Skip.
-  - **Saved questions:** they now stand on their own.
-  - **Primer:** for newcomers.
-  - **Reset:** start over easily as a new user.
-  - **Test-traffic tagging:** your own testing stays out of the numbers.
-- Transcripts of every session are in `transcripts/`.
-**Draft:**

I started from my own understanding of how people learn. It comes from my background as a professional tutor and a long-standing personal interest in education and what actually helps people learn. I wrote that down as nine design principles. Then I had Claude check each one against peer-reviewed research, so the foundation rested on evidence and not only my experience.

Next, I designed the product experience myself and shared it with Claude. We went back and forth on whether it made sense, and I made the final calls. Every meaningful choice went into a decision log with the alternatives I considered (60+ entries).

Finally, I tested the experience myself in a real browser and played through it as a user. As AI takes on more of the intermediate work, I think the most important thing for a person to check is the final result, so that's where I spent my review time. Those playthroughs drove a second build round. The biggest change came when I got a question I couldn't answer and the product had no way to help me learn it. So I added hints, "Teach me", and "Ask Claude" to every question; slightly less credit after help; and the answer revealed only after you've tried. Now people at any level can take part, not just those who already know.
## 3. How it enhances, not replaces, human agency
-**The brief asks:** how the design keeps the human an active participant.
-**Questions to answer:**
-- Where does the learner make the real decisions in the work?
-- What can the learner always control or opt out of?
-- Why do it this way instead of having Claude just explain things?
-**Raw material:**

-- **P7 "The user stays the decision-maker":** at real forks (which metric, where to set the threshold), Claude asks with a *decide* moment and then builds on the answer ("You picked recall, so I scored the models on that").
-- **Structural pause:** a learning moment is a tool call that ends Claude's turn, so Claude *cannot* answer its own question.
-- **Learning by consequence:** if a choice is weak but safe, Claude follows it and lets the real results show the effect.
-- **Control:**
-  - Skip, "Quiz me later", or report any question.
-  - Optional guardrails (Light / Balanced / Strict).
-  - Bosses are opt-in ("Take it on / Keep working"), can be skipped, or turned off.
-  - Typing past a question simply skips it.
-- **Help is learner-initiated:** hints, Teach me, and Ask Claude. The answer appears only after an attempt (or after asking twice), so the learner still does the thinking.
-- Sources: `docs/design-principles.md` P7, P8; `docs/design-plan.md` §3, §15.
-**Draft:**

At its core, what I built is an interactive question-and-answer system woven into real work. As you work with Claude, it stops at meaningful points and asks you a question: a decision to make, a prediction, a concept to apply. The questions get harder as you get them right, because the engine aims for about 80% success. Each stretch of work builds to a boss battle, a short run of tougher questions on what you've just done. So at the heart of the experience, the person has to take agency, answering harder and harder problems instead of watching Claude solve them.

The design follows two of my core principles: "active application is the core" and "the user stays the decision-maker." The learner should be thinking about the problem, not receiving a firehose of information. At real forks, like which metric to optimize or where to set a threshold, Claude asks instead of deciding. Then it builds on the answer: "You picked recall, so I scored the models on that." Making decisions uses a different part of the brain than taking in facts. It leaves people feeling empowered, not like a store of knowledge, and storing knowledge is something AI is increasingly good at anyway.

The control I care about most is that help only comes when you ask for it. Hints, "Teach me", and "Ask Claude" are always there, but nothing appears unless the learner reaches for it, and the answer is revealed only after an attempt. That puts the learner in control of the difficulty, including the choice to struggle through a problem on their own. Everything else is opt-out too: skip a question, save it with "Quiz me later", turn down a boss, or keep typing and the question steps aside.
## 4. Learning principles behind the decisions
-**The brief asks:** the learning principles behind your decisions.
-**Questions to answer:**
-- Which 3–5 principles matter most to you, and where does each show up in the product?
-- Which research findings shaped specific numbers or rules?
-**Raw material:**
-- **Retrieval practice:** free recall first, with multiple choice only as a fallback.
-- **Immediate explanatory feedback:** every answer gets a "why". Mistakes help only with an immediate explanation (Kornell, Hays & Bjork 2009).

-- **Desirable difficulty, banded:** target success rates are first exposure 85–90%, practice 75–85%, boss 65–80%. Elo-style mastery backs off fast after misses and ramps up slowly (P5, `reference/research/01-challenge-ratio.md`).
-- **Just-in-time learning:** moments are triggered by the learner's own work and data, not a curriculum.
-- **Interleaving:** bosses mix concepts from the session.
-- **Spaced review:** concepts you struggled with come back in a later session.
-- **Scaffolding without spoon-feeding:** hints → lesson with a worked example → ask; less credit after help; reveal only after an attempt.
-- **Motivation without punishment:** proportional rewards (XP, sounds, confetti, level-ups that unlock themes); wrong answers get a soft sound and encouraging copy (P2).

-- **Cut after playtesting (2026-10-18):** serialized story chapters (after bosses and at wrap-up). Dinakar couldn't follow them while working, and in Co-learn the work itself is what engages people, so the story competed with it (and added a wait of up to 25s after each boss). It's switched off per mode, not deleted, and planned for Learn mode, where there's no real work to carry engagement.
-- **Code paces, Claude creates (P8):** a small deterministic engine decides when and how hard; Claude writes the questions and grades the answers.
-**Draft:**
Three principles matter most to me, and each shows up directly in the product.

**1. Practice.** People learn by applying knowledge, not by reading about it. This principle covers several research findings at once, and it's why questions are the backbone of both modes. Learners recall the answer themselves before seeing options; multiple choice is only a fallback. Every answer, right or wrong, gets an immediate "why", because mistakes only help when they're explained right away (Kornell, Hays & Bjork, 2009). Bosses mix concepts from across the session, and concepts you struggled with come back in a later session.

**3. Reward.** Hard work should feel rewarded. XP, sounds, confetti, and level-ups that unlock themes celebrate success in proportion to the effort. Wrong answers get a soft sound and encouragement, never a penalty. In Learn mode, a serialized story adds a reason to keep going. Together they keep a positive feedback loop running: effort leads to reward, which leads to more effort.
## 5. Measuring success
-**The brief asks:** how you'd measure success.
-**Questions to answer:**
-- What does "success" mean for a learner (in the session and later), and for the product?
-- Which metrics would you watch first, and what would make you change the design?
-**Raw material:**
-- **`/insights`** (built; anonymous; test traffic excluded) shows:
-  - answer, skip, defer and reveal rates
-  - help usage, and scores with vs without help
-  - accuracy against the P5 bands (too easy / in band / too hard)
-  - boss offered / declined / skipped / outcomes
-  - pacing-gate decisions
-  - wrap-up "Did you learn something?" 👍 rate
-  - **delayed retention** (score on the same concept in later sessions vs the first)
-  - daily totals
-- **Most important:** delayed retention, plus task completion (people still finish their work). Session XP is not a success metric.
-- **Early signal from testing:** questions landed *above* the target band (too easy), which is a tuning input.
-- **Future:** A/B the guardrail defaults; tune boss frequency from offered/declined rates.
-**Draft:**

For the product, success means it actually helps people learn. By the end of a session, people should be able to answer questions and apply the knowledge the product tests them on. The best measure of that is how often people answer correctly, especially at the end of a session in the boss battle, which mixes concepts from the whole session into harder questions. A strong boss score is good evidence that the material actually stuck. Alongside that, I'd measure how confident people feel about what they learned with a short survey. The wrap-up already asks a quick "Did you learn something?"
For users, success also includes how they feel: whether they enjoyed it and want to keep using it. At scale, that's daily active users and return rates.

Together these show where to tune the experience to be easier or harder. The dashboard also measures delayed retention, comparing scores on a concept in a later session with the first, which is the clearest test of whether learning lasted.
## 6. Scaling to millions of users
-**The brief asks:** how this would scale.
-**Questions to answer:**
-- What's expensive, and how does the design keep it cheap?
-- What would have to change for a real launch?
-**Raw material:**
-- **Stateless serverless routes:** the server owns state in Redis; per-user state is small JSON.
-- **Cost controls:**
-  - Prompt caching on the system prompt, tools and history.
-  - Cheap fast models where possible (Haiku for grading, verification and hints).
-  - The pacing engine is deterministic code (no model cost).
-  - Long sessions use the API's on-demand compaction.
-- **Measured cost:** about $0.20–0.30 per 10-minute demo session.
-- **Abuse protection:** rate limits (20 per minute per browser, 60 per IP), daily spend caps ($5 / $25 / $75), and limits that fail open with an owner alert.
-- **The sandbox is Anthropic-managed:** each session gets its own code-execution container.
-- **For a real launch:**
-  - accounts instead of anonymous cookies (cross-device)
-  - relax the demo-only boss nudge
-  - tune defaults from data
-  - more surfaces (see §7)
-- Sources: `docs/design-plan.md` §9.3, §11, §15; `docs/backlog.md`.
-**Draft:**

The hardest part of scaling isn't infrastructure; it's that every learner is different. People need Claude to sound and speak to them differently, and they differ in how hard the content should be and how fast it should ramp up. One model serving everyone the same way won't work. The prototype already adapts difficulty per person with a small engine, but at scale I'd push further. First, I'd prompt the model to adapt as much as possible to each user. Then I'd add persistent personalization that carries across sessions, potentially using lightweight fine-tuning such as LoRA if prompting isn't enough.

The architecture is a reasonable starting point. The server routes are stateless, so they scale out easily; each user's state is a small JSON record in Upstash Redis. Costs stay low through prompt caching, a cheaper model (Haiku) for grading and hints, a pacing engine that is plain code with no model calls, and automatic summarizing of long sessions. A 10-minute session costs about $0.20–0.30 today. Rate limits and daily spend caps protect against abuse.
- **UX polish:** refine the design so each element sits in the ideal spot.
- **Model quality:** iterate on every stage of the experience so the questions, hints, and explanations are as good as they can be.
## 7. Getting a sister team to adopt it long-term
-**The brief asks:** how a sister team would adopt this.
-**Questions to answer:**
-- What is the reusable piece another Claude surface could adopt?
-- What would you hand them (contract, engine, UI), and how would you make adoption low-effort?
-- How would you keep it working over time (shared mastery, metrics, ownership)?
-**Raw material:**

-- **The `learning_moment` tool + pacing engine is a surface-agnostic contract.** Any Claude surface (Claude Code as a `/co-learn` mode, Claude.ai as a toggle) adopts it by adding the tool and rendering the card.
-- The engine is pure, unit-tested TypeScript (`web/lib/engine/`) with a clear API (`EngineApi` in `web/lib/contracts/engine.ts`).
-- A shared mastery profile could follow users across surfaces, so review would work everywhere.
-- Telemetry events + `/insights` give a sister team the same success metrics out of the box.
-- Sources: `docs/design-plan.md` §15; `web/lib/contracts/*`.
-**Draft:**
I read this question two ways: a sister team *using* Co-learn in their own work, or a sister team *building it into* their own product. I'll answer both.

**Using it.** I'd start by learning what the team works on and asking them to share a recent problem that was complex or ambiguous. Then I'd build a demo showing how Co-learn would have helped them work through that problem and learn along the way. A demo on their own real problem is far more convincing than a generic pitch.
## Remaining for Dinakar (before the Oct 21, 9:00 AM PT deadline)

-- [ ] **Written design rationale** (`docs/design-rationale.md`, in your voice). The scaffold has headers, questions, and raw material. Run `/rationale-coach` in Claude Code for a guided, section-by-section session.

• It's opt-in, and "Keep working" never blocks the work.
• Rewards scale with the milestone: small sound → jingle → boss win with confetti (P2, it feels like a game). |

Show the kind decline. | • This came from my own playtest: I hit a question I couldn't answer and had no way to learn it. Questions alone aren't enough.

• Reward: XP, sounds, confetti, level-ups. Hard work should feel rewarded; that keeps the learning loop running. |

| **3:10–3:45** Wrap-up | **Tab D** (a finished session). Click "See the wrap-up": Codex of concepts, "Review next time", XP/level, "Learn more" readings, "Next time you could…". | • You leave with a record: what you learned, what to review (it resurfaces in the next session), and real readings with links.
• Sources everywhere Claude explains a concept, so learners can verify (P9, trustworthy content). |

-| **3:45–4:20** Learn mode coda **[B1]** | **Tab E** (`/learn`, Roman Republic): path card at the top, a cited lesson, a question after it, a story chapter. | • The same engine generalizes to pure topic learning: a 3-part path, ~120-word cited lessons, a question after each, bosses as chapter tests.
• Story chapters live *here*, not in Co-learn. Playtesting showed a story competed with real work, so I cut it there (a design call driven by testing). |

• The story lives *here*. In Co-learn it competed with the real work, so I cut it there after playtesting. |

| **4:20–4:55** How it works (internals) | The **"How it works" diagram** below (screenshot it, or open this doc on GitHub). Optionally flash `web/lib/claude/work/loop.ts` and `web/lib/engine/` in the repo. | • Browser → a Next.js route on Vercel (`/api/chat`) → the **Claude API**, streamed back live. One work turn is a streaming tool loop on the Anthropic SDK (Sonnet 5.5; Opus for the session plan, Haiku for grading and quick hints).
• Claude has Anthropic's **server-side tools**: code execution (real Python in Anthropic's sandbox) and web search (citations become the [n] source links).
• Plus **my own tools**: `learning_moment` (Claude proposes a question), `milestone_reached` (a chunk of work is done → boss); in Learn mode `set_learning_path` and `teach`.
• **"Code paces, Claude creates" (P8):** Claude only *proposes* a moment; a small deterministic engine (`lib/engine/`, plain unit-tested TypeScript) decides whether it shows, how hard, XP and mastery. No model call for pacing.
• State and telemetry live in Upstash Redis; long histories are compacted (above ~40k tokens); daily spend caps ($5 per browser, $25 per IP, $75 global) and rate limits protect the key. |

-| **4:55–5:30** Process **[B2]** | Repo on GitHub: `docs/design-principles.md`, then `docs/decision-log.md` (scroll). | • Principles first, before choosing the option, so the option was chosen for learning reasons.
• Research-backed decisions (challenge bands, code execution) and a decision log with alternatives for each.
• Built with Claude Code: I owned the decisions, Claude proposed options.
• Playtest → change: story removed, questions moved to the real fork, help tools added. *(Pick 1–2 examples from your rationale.)* |

+| **4:55–5:30** Process **[B2]** | Repo on GitHub: `docs/design-principles.md`, then `docs/decision-log.md` (scroll). | • I started from my own understanding of learning, from tutoring professionally and a long interest in education. I wrote it as principles, then had Claude check each against peer-reviewed research.
• I designed the product and pressure-tested it with Claude; every decision is logged with alternatives.
• As a Staff engineer I wrote the engineering plan (contracts, parallel build order); Claude executed it.
• My check was the final product: as AI does more of the intermediate work, the result is what a person should validate. So I played through it and drove a second build round. |

| **5:30–5:55** Principles recap **[B4]** | Back to the app: Settings (gear) → guardrails Light/Balanced/Strict. | • Targets about 80% correct (85–90% for new concepts, 65–80% for bosses); back off fast after misses.
• No quota by default: a quality bar decides; opt-in guardrails for fewer interruptions. |

-| **5:55–6:30** Measuring success **[B5]** | `/insights` (Settings → "How Co-learn is doing"). Point at the answer/skip rates, P5 band adherence, delayed retention, and the 👍 rate. | • Success means people **still finish their work** *and* **remember later**: delayed retention on resurfaced concepts is the headline number, not XP.
• Watch skip/defer rates for over-interruption and band adherence for difficulty.
• Early signal: questions were landing above the band (too easy), which is a tuning input.
• Next: A/B the guardrail defaults. |

-| **6:30–6:50** Scaling **[B6]** | Stay on `/insights`. | • Stateless serverless routes, small per-user state, prompt caching, cheap models for grading/hints, the engine costs nothing.
• About $0.20–0.30 per 10-minute session today, with spend caps and rate limits.
• For launch: real accounts, tune defaults from data. |

-| **6:50–7:15** Sister-team adoption **[B7]** | `web/lib/contracts/` in the repo (the `learning_moment` tool and `EngineApi`). | • The reusable piece is a **tool contract + pacing engine**: any surface (Claude Code as `/co-learn`, Claude.ai as a toggle) adds the tool and renders the card.
• A shared mastery profile follows the user across surfaces; the same events give them `/insights` out of the box.
• Future: a local bridge so moments run inside your own Claude Code session. |

+| **5:55–6:30** Measuring success **[B5]** | `/insights` (Settings → "How Co-learn is doing"). Point at the band accuracy, boss outcomes, help usage, and the 👍 rate. | • Success = people actually learn: accuracy on questions, especially the **end-of-session boss**, is the best evidence it stuck. Plus a confidence survey (the wrap-up asks "Did you learn something?").
• For users: do they enjoy it and come back? First I'd check adoption and retention (DAU, returners).
• Then in-session signals: accuracy vs the difficulty bands (early testing: too easy), boss take-on rate, help usage. They tell me where to make it easier or harder. Delayed retention shows whether it lasted. |

+| **6:30–6:50** Scaling **[B6]** | Stay on `/insights`. | • The hard part is people, not servers: everyone needs a different tone, difficulty and ramp. So: more adaptive prompting, persistent personalization across sessions, maybe LoRA if prompting isn't enough.
• The architecture is a good start: stateless routes, prompt caching, Haiku for grading, a free pacing engine; ~$0.20–0.30 per session.
• For launch: off the free tiers, ideally onto Anthropic's own infrastructure; built into Claude or a standalone product; UX polish; iterate on question and hint quality. |

+| **6:50–7:15** Sister-team adoption **[B7]** | `web/lib/contracts/` in the repo (the `learning_moment` tool and `EngineApi`). | • Two readings. *Using it:* ask them for a recent complex problem and build a demo of Co-learn on it.
• *Building it in:* start with a team building custom Claude interfaces. Pitch: making Claude game-like pays off beyond learning. Share the question cards, the game layer (one tool + the engine), and the metrics/`/insights`.
• Our team keeps maintaining the infrastructure; both teams share ownership of the user metrics. |

| **7:15–7:30** Close | Back to the landing page. | • One line: Claude does the work *with* you, and you come out more capable.
• Thanks. |
## How it works (diagram for the 4:20 segment)
Note: test tabs show a small "Test traffic (this tab)" badge in the corner. It's fine to leave it, or mention it in one breath.
## Recording checklist
-- [ ] Update the talking points from the finished `docs/design-rationale.md`.
- [ ] All tabs above staged and checked (reload each once).
- [ ] Browser: one window, zoom 110–125% so the text reads on video; bookmarks bar hidden; notifications off (Focus mode).
- [ ] Sound on for the unlock and boss sounds (check the recorder captures system audio, or mention the sounds).

# Co-learn: Anthropic Education Labs take-home (Full Stack Engineer)

**Co-learn** is a Claude mode where a professional does real work with Claude and comes out more capable.
Claude collaborates on the task normally, including running real code. At high-value moments it pauses
and turns the work into a short challenge the learner solves themselves. The learner's answers steer the work.

- **Live prototype:** https://anthropic-take-home-10-17-26.vercel.app (the access password is in the submission)
- **Try it:**
  1. Type `/co-learn`.
  2. Click **Try the demo: train a churn model** and pick a familiarity and time (10 min).
  3. Or type `/learn` for **Learn mode** (study a topic with Claude as a tutor) and try the sample: the fall of the Roman Republic.
- **Option chosen:** B, learning through collaboration with Claude
- **Deadline:** Oct 21, 2026, 9:00 AM PT

## What's in the prototype
- **The work loop:**
  - Claude (Sonnet 5.5) works in Anthropic's code-execution sandbox on a seeded churn dataset: real code, real metrics, real charts.
  - It proposes learning moments through a `learning_moment` tool (decide / predict / explain back / spot the issue / fill the gap).
  - A small deterministic **pacing engine** (`web/lib/engine/`) decides which moments to show and how hard they are. Mastery is Elo-style, with target success bands.
- **Answering:**
  - Free-form answers first, graded with a short "why".
  - A multiple-choice fallback after a miss.
  - Predictions are graded against the real code output.
- **Sources you can check:** Claude web-searches before explaining a concept; cited sentences get [n] markers with links. Every session ends with **Learn more**: 3-5 real readings from a search (links are never written from memory).
- **Learn mode** (`/learn`): the same engine, question cards, help, bosses and Codex, with Claude as a tutor: a short reorderable path of parts, a ~120-word cited lesson then a question each time, and story chapters as boss rewards.
- **Help when stuck:**
  - Hints, **Teach me** (a short lesson with a worked example), and **Ask Claude**.
  - The answer is revealed only after an attempt, or after asking twice.
  - Help reduces credit.
- **Game layer:**
  - XP and levels (themes and sound packs unlock).
  - Optional **boss** challenges at milestones ("Take it on / Keep working", or "Skip this boss").
  - Story chapters as boss rewards in Learn mode only (in Co-learn the work itself carries engagement).
  - A wrap-up with a quiz of saved questions, a Codex of concepts, and suggestions for next time.
- **Across sessions:**
  - The **Codex** (`/codex`) tracks every concept.
  - Concepts due for review are passed to the next session.
- **Measuring success:** `/insights` shows anonymous, aggregate usage:
  - answer, skip and help rates
  - accuracy against the target bands
  - boss outcomes
  - small-sample retention

## Repo layout
| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `web/` | The app (Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind v4, `@anthropic-ai/sdk`, Upstash Redis); see `web/README.md` |
| `docs/design-rationale.md` | Written design rationale (deliverable) |
| `docs/decision-log.md` | Every meaningful decision, the alternatives, and the reasoning |
| `docs/design-principles.md` | The design principles the product is built on |
| `docs/design-plan.md` | Build blueprint: architecture, work loop, moments, engine, data model |
| `docs/product-vision.md`, `docs/context-persistence.md` | Product vision; storage and model-context plan |
| `docs/plan.md`, `docs/HANDOFF.md` | Timeline and checklists; session handoffs (including a manual testing guide) |
| `docs/backlog.md` | Untriaged ideas for later |
| `docs/assignment-brief.md` | Summary of the assignment |
| `reference/` | Research reports and reference sheets |
| `transcripts/` | Claude Code transcripts (required for submission) |
| `alternative-projects/` | Earlier ideas, not part of the submission |
| `CLAUDE.md` | Context and working agreements for Claude Code |

## Run locally
```bash
cd web
cp .env.example .env.local   # add ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (+ Upstash KV_* vars, or it falls back to an in-memory store)
npm ci
npm run dev                  # http://localhost:3000
npm run typecheck && npm test && npm run lint && npm run build
```

## Deliverables checklist
- [x] Deployed, working prototype using the Claude API
- [x] Code in this GitHub repo
- [ ] Written design rationale (`docs/design-rationale.md`)
- [ ] Video walkthrough, ≤ 8 minutes, with screenshare
- [ ] Complete Claude transcripts (`transcripts/`)
- [ ] Submitted via Greenhouse
